title: Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist
description: Kids tend to express their emotions in actions. Toddlers scream and hit when they don't get their way. Middle schoolers stomp out of the room when the
body: Kids tend to express their emotions in actions. Toddlers scream and hit when they don't get their way. Middle schoolers stomp out of the room when they get angry. Teenagers roll their eyes and slam doors to express frustration or disapproval. As a psychologist and co-author of "Parents Have Feelings, Too," I've worked with hundreds of parents who feel overwhelmed when their child doesn't listen, misbehaves or throws tantrums for no discernible reason. Some of them try to negotiate with their children. Others become frustrated and lose their cool. Both approaches can leave parents feeling even more taxed and out of control. Misbehaving is a normal part of childhood. And it's a form of communication, like a set of clues to the scary feelings and worries behind the meltdowns. Parents who can follow their children's clues and address their underlying emotions set kids up for long-term success. These kids become more emotionally intelligent, which helps them weather setbacks, embrace independence and try new things. The next time your child acts out, try doing these five things. 1. Calm yourself firstWhether your toddler is having a tantrum or your teenager is yelling at you, it's normal to feel rattled and even lose your cool. But children learn by witnessing what we do, so try to stay calm amid the chaos. Pause and take five deep belly breaths. This might sound simple, but deep breathing delivers oxygen to our muscles, which helps elicit the body's relaxation response. Emotions are contagious, which means that when parents remain calm, kids "catch" their calm and learn how to regulate their own big feelings. 2. Act like a detective, not a CEOWhen kids act up, you may be tempted to tell your child to "knock it off!" Or you might jump into problem-solving mode. But taking charge can cause kids to shut down and hurt their self-confidence. Instead of acting like a CEO, approach the situation like a detective. Try to adopt a curious mindset, asking yourself: "What might be going on for my kid right now that's driving this behavior?" For example, a child who lies may be afraid of getting into trouble, while a teen who rejects boundaries may want more independence. Let your child know that telling the truth will always be applauded, and invite your boundary-pushing teen to brainstorm with you about the things they want. When you identify the underlying driver, you've solved the mystery, which is more than half the battle. 3. Help your child name their emotionsA child's misbehavior can be what psychologists call a "defense." Defenses — like being dishonest, avoiding, criticizing others and misdirecting anger — are brilliant ways we protect ourselves from painful emotions.Defenses temporarily numb potent feelings like shame, guilt or sadness, but they don't help kids "feel and deal" with life's challenges in the long run. Finding language for our feelings is called "emotion naming," which helps calm down the brain's amygdala and take the edge off big feelings. Try to help your child name the emotions that their defenses cover up. Simply asking "Are you sad?" "Are you angry?" or "Are you worried?" is a good start. 4. Investigate if your behavior plays a role Children imitate behaviors that they witness at school and at home. If your child's misbehavior keeps repeating, reflect on your own actions. Ask yourself: "How do I cope with my own emotions?" "What do I do when I feel angry, sad, anxious or fearful?""Do I use defenses to cope with painful emotions instead of dealing with them?""Does my child's behavior mirror my own?" Simply taking a moment to identify and validate your own emotions and seek what you need goes a long way.  Begin by scanning your body from head to toe. What sensations do you notice? A heaviness in your chest can be a sign of sadness, and may mean you need support from your partner or a friend. Anger, on the other hand, can make your body temperature rise and your jaw feel tense, and might indicate you need to set a boundary, take time for self-care or address a problem.5. Consider how unresolved stress plays a role Daily as well as prolonged stress affect the mind and body. Stressors can rattle a child's nervous system, making it harder for them to regulate their emotions.As a psychologist, I know that this dysregulation can affect how a child behaves. It's why kids often regress when a new baby is born or when they go through a tough transition. It's also why kids often melt down when they're overtired.The acronym "H.A.L.T." — which stands for hungry, angry, lonely or tired — can help parents pinpoint underlying stressors that may be making it harder for kids to regulate their feelings and leading them to act out.Try meeting their needs first and see if their behavior shifts. A well-timed snack, nap or quality time can be the perfect reset. Juli Fraga is a licensed psychologist with nearly two decades of experience working with new parents. She is a co-author of the book "Parents Have Feelings, Too." She also teaches workshops for expectant parents at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) hospital, where she also supervises psychiatry residents. Follow her on Instagram @parentshavefeelingstoo.

title: Treasury yields face 4.8% test as fiscal risks threaten to spill into other assets
description: A trader works on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Aug. 24, 2026. Brendan Mcdermid | ReutersTreasury yields fac
body: A trader works on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Aug. 24, 2026. Brendan Mcdermid | ReutersTreasury yields face a key test at 4.8%, with a sustained move above that level potentially creating "meaningful problems" for other asset classes, according to Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co. "We remain concerned about the Treasury market…as rising fiscal deficits, massive debt issuance, and heavy corporate borrowing continue to pressure long-term yields... while Treasury Department jawboning has failed to produce the desired decline in rates (at least so far)," Maley said in a note over the weekend.A sustained move above 4.8% on the 10-year Treasury yield — which marks the the high reached in January 2025 — "would be particularly concerning," he said, as it could begin to create broader problems for markets and signal that fiscal concerns are overwhelming policymakers' attempts to influence borrowing costs.Maley said recent efforts by the U.S. Treasury Department and Secretary Scott Bessent to talk yields lower have so far failed to generate the desired response. The effort came as investors were heavily short Treasurys and summer trading conditions were relatively thin, with policymakers hoping verbal intervention could trigger a meaningful bond rally.Instead, the episode underscores the growing difficulty of addressing market concerns without tackling the underlying fiscal pressures, he highlighted. The U.S. budget deficit and national debt, now above $40 trillion, are becoming increasingly difficult for investors to ignore, while the government is competing with large volumes of corporate borrowing for investor demand.More than $8.4 trillion of U.S. government securities are scheduled to roll over between now and year-end, while September could be a record month for high-grade corporate issuance, according to Maley. Goldman Sachs recently revised its forecast for USD investment-grade issuance in 2026 upward to $2.3 trillion. The pressure is not confined to the U.S. Japan, the U.K., France and other developed economies face significant fiscal challenges, adding to a broader shift in global bond markets as investors demand greater compensation for absorbing government debt."None of this means the bond market will move in a straight line," Maley said, noting that bearish sentiment and stretched positioning could still trigger a sharp rally in Treasury futures. Any such move, however, could prove tactical rather than mark a reversal of the longer-term trend.The 5% level has become widely watched for the long end of the Treasury curve, but Maley said the market's thresholds have repeatedly shifted higher, from 4.4% to 4.5%, 4.6% and 4.7%.A sustained break above 4.8% could have repercussions well beyond bonds. Michael Chen, general manager of Noah ARK Hong Kong, said a disorderly rise in long-term Treasury yields could trigger repricing across assets that depend on long-term cash flows, including ultra-long-duration bonds, high-valuation growth stocks, commercial real estate and some private assets.Chen said the structural pressure on Treasurys was building as fiscal dominance pushes investors to demand greater risk compensation for holding long-term debt. He favors gold and hard currency as structural hedges and is underweight ultra-long-duration Treasurys, while maintaining exposure to quality equities, real assets and AI-related physical infrastructure such as electricity, power grids, energy storage and data centers.HSBC has also turned more cautious on long-dated developed-market bonds. The bank raised its end-2026 forecast for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.65% from 4.30%, citing a higher structural floor under long-term yields and a more hawkish distribution of potential monetary-policy outcomes.HSBC said it remains cautious on long-end bonds across developed markets, while also raising its end-2026 forecast for 10-year German Bund yields to 3% from 2.8%.For Maley, the key issue is that any near-term decline in yields would not necessarily resolve the longer-term problem."If we get a bounce in the Treasury market soon (and thus a drop in yields)…and even if it can last through the mid-term election…it's not something that can be softened over the longer-term…without some serious changes on the fiscal front," he said.

title: I'm a nutritionist from Japan: 7 'essential' anti-inflammatory foods that I swear by
description: Feeling off physically can make it harder to do everything else in life that matters to you. Relationships and work can suffer, and your goals can get
body: Feeling off physically can make it harder to do everything else in life that matters to you. Relationships and work can suffer, and your goals can get put on the back burner while you put yourself to rights.We often don't realize the influence inflammation can have on many aspects of our health. It can affect your cognitive ability and memory and it can be a factor in ailments like arthritis, ulcerative colitis, heart disease, metabolic disorder, diabetes, and some autoimmune issues and cancers. I'm a nutritionist from Nara, Japan, and I like to recommend traditional Japanese ingredients to my clients. These foods are rich in essential nutrients that can help fight inflammation, improve immune system function and boost focus and energy — so people can do the things they care about the most.I swear by these seven foods, which you can find not just at Asian markets, but increasingly at your local grocery store, too. Of course, make sure you talk to your doctor before making any major changes to your diet.1. Konjac Konnyaku is a popular Japanese jelly made from a root vegetable called konjac. You can also make noodles from the jelly, a dish called shirataki, which translates to "white waterfall" because of the appearance of the noodles. Konnyaku is calorie-free and rich in glucomannan, a soluble fiber that helps with digestion. During the traditional preparation process, calcium is added, which gives the jelly its distinctive firm and rubbery texture. Konnyaku, seaweed, mushrooms and tofu, all in one quick meal.Photo: Michiko TomiokaAt home, I like to add the konnyaku jelly to cooked vegetables. Shirataki noodles work well in soups, stir-fries, hot pots, cold noodle dishes, and ramen-style bowls. One of the best things about konnyaku is that it has almost no flavor of its own, and it absorbs the taste of whatever you cook it with. I often recommend this ingredient to clients who are thinking about weight management. Some delicious shirataki noodles.Photo: Michiko Tomioka2. Burdock root Burdock root, known in Japan as gobo, may look like a stick you might find in the woods, but there are many delicious uses for it.It's a traditional Japanese root vegetable with a strong nutrition profile. It is high in a soluble fiber called inulin, which helps promote overall gut health and digestion. At home, I like to chop it and add it to miso soup and serve it with nimono (simmered dishes), salad, and fries. The rich flavor of the root complements the other ingredients. 3. Seaweed Seaweed appears in many Japanese dishes and snacks. It's low in calories and rich in minerals, fiber, vitamins, and polyphenols, all of which help fight inflammation. Lately, my top seaweeds for home cooking are nori and wakame. They are affordable and available at most grocery stores. Some of my favorite seaweed dishes include nori-wrapped rice balls, mochi, sushi and wakame salad.A miso soup packed with wakame, veggies, tofu and shiitake mushrooms.Photo: Michiko Tomioka4. Fermented soy and rice  One of the great benefits of Japanese cooking is the regular inclusion of fermented foods like miso (soybean paste), natto (fermented soybeans) and nukazuke (vegetables pickled with fermented rice bran). Natto contains probiotics and prebiotics which can help support the gut microbiome and digestion. It's also high in plant-based protein and vitamins like K2, which helps strengthen your bones. Without natto, miso soup, and pickles, my breakfast does not feel complete. I also enjoy natto with seaweed, oatmeal, and whole grain bread.A dish of natto, vinegar, and nukazuke topped with shiso.Photo: Michiko Tomioka5. Dried bonito flakesI love an ingredient called katsuobushi. It's skipjack tuna that's been simmered, smoked, dried, and traditionally fermented until it becomes extremely hard, almost like stone. Then it's shaved down into flakes. It's a long cooking process that removes most of the moisture and fat. What remains is a concentrated protein and deep umami flavor. I use bonito flakes and kombu seaweed to make dashi broth. I also sprinkle them over tofu or salad, and mix them into rice balls for a simple, comforting boost of flavor.  6. Mushrooms Shiitake, maitake, enokidake, and shimeji mushroom varieties each offer distinct flavors, textures, and nutritional benefits. And they are generally low in calories. For example, 100 grams of raw shiitake mushrooms provides about 34 calories, three grams of fiber, and two and a half grams of protein — all cholesterol free. I like to keep dried mushrooms in my kitchen and use them in curries, soups, and dressings. They have a wonderful umami flavor and are also enjoyable on their own.  7. Green tea I've always had some type of green tea with each meal, even as a small child. Since green tea is usually enjoyed without milk or sugar, it's nearly calorie-free. It also contains antioxidants that can help support immune and metabolic function. My morning ritual. Matcha and a view.Photo: Michiko TomiokaAfter brewing my tea, I'll prepare a small salad with the used tea leaves and vinegar or miso dressing. I also regularly practice the traditional Japanese tea ceremony for preparing matcha. It's a part of my daily ritual and it fills me with joy and a sense of peace. Michiko Tomioka, MBA, RDN is a certified nutritionist and longevity expert. Born and raised in Nara, Japan, her approach focuses on a plant-based diet. She has worked in nutritional roles at substance recovery centers, charter schools and food banks. Follow her on Instagram @michian_rd.

title: Icons Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem never officially retired—why that's a choice for some and requirement for others
description: I and many others looked forward to a luncheon with Dress for Success, a women's workforce development organization, at the end of September. Gloria S
body: I and many others looked forward to a luncheon with Dress for Success, a women's workforce development organization, at the end of September. Gloria Steinem was scheduled to be the keynote speaker sharing her insights on "the importance of empowering women to create meaningful change," per the invitation. Steinem died on Wednesday."Gloria's unwavering commitment to women's equality, opportunity, and empowerment helped shape generations of changemakers and inspired countless individuals to raise their voices, pursue their ambitions, and challenge barriers," Joanie Bily, CEO of Dress for Success Worldwide, said in a statement provided to CNBC Make It. The organization plans to pay tribute to Steinem's "life, legacy and impact" at the luncheon.The news of Steinem's death shocked and saddened me and many around the world who have since shared tributes. A trailblazing icon of the feminist movement, Steinem will be remembered for her journalistic pursuits — co-founding Ms. Magazine and New York Magazine — along with her staunch activism pushing for women's civil and reproductive rights.Steinem's health had declined recently, according to the Associated Press, but she hadn't publicly disclosed an illness or given other health updates that may have made her passing seem less sudden. In a similar fashion back in May, Dolly Parton revealed some health issues in a video posted to Instagram and announced she was canceling a Las Vegas residency slated for September. She said she still needed time to heal and couldn't yet perform, but assured her fans she was still working. Parton died on August 25.Both Steinem and Parton were busy until the very end. On top of the upcoming luncheon appearance, Steinem recently finished a memoir scheduled for release on Sept. 22. Parton, "worked up until the day she died," her longtime manager, Danny Nozell, said in an Aug. 26 press release. She was involved in numerous projects before her death including a biopic and musical documentary, he said. She also made sure those projects would be left in trusted hands. The women, well past traditional retirement ages — Parton at 80 and Steinem at 92 — were among millions of Americans who, for various reasons, continue working after they've technically retired or can start claiming their full Social Security retirement benefits. That's between ages 66 and 67, depending on when you were born, and increases for every year you delay claiming until age 70.Why people who can retire sometimes don'tFor some Americans, working in retirement or even up to their death, isn't a choice. Around 41% of working retirees who gave a reason say they need the money to make ends meet, according to the Employee Benefit Research Institute's 2026 Retirement Confidence survey. The survey polled 1,045 retirees in January with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.We don't know the details of their personal financial situations, but Parton and Steinem likely could have stopped working and, given their storied careers, were probably not doing it for whatever paychecks they may have earned from their late-in-life endeavors. Both certainly worked less in their final years than during the peaks of their careers, but continued giving interviews, making appearances and pursuing their creative passions. "With people like Gloria and Dolly, I'm not sure 'work' captures the whole story," says Danielle Robay, host of the "Question Everything" and "Bookmarked" podcasts, and a Gloria Steinem Foundation fellow. "When your work is so closely connected to your purpose, creativity, relationships, and way of understanding the world, continuing may not feel like an obligation. It may feel like being fully alive."That aligns with millions of working retirees who stay in the workforce for non-monetary reasons. Some 91% of working retirees report holding jobs to stay active and involved and 85% say they work because they enjoy it, per the EBRI survey.Kelly Klingaman, an Austin, Texas-based certified financial planner, says her clients — who are primarily millennial women — feel similarly and "don't want to fully remove themselves from work." She suspects that's more of an ambition-driven mindset."There aren't a ton of women who have done what they've done before them, and it's tough for them to imagine backing out completely when they've got a chance to inspire other women to pursue a similar path in their industry," she says.Regardless of their reasons for wanting to stay in the workforce, many Americans would prefer to treat late in life work as a choice rather than a necessity, says Scott Boyles, a CFP also based in Austin. "Getting to the point where 'working is optional' is the idea of retirement," he says. "If you enjoy what you do, want to start another career, volunteer, consult, or maybe even open a business well into your 70s, that's great. The financial plan should give you the freedom to make that decision," he says.'Financial independence is the finish line'The key to affording that freedom, Boyles says, is focusing less on a goal retirement age, and more on figuring out what it actually costs to fund your life. That means estimating your expenses — including living costs, remaining debt payments and future medical bills — and weighing those against how much you'll be able to bring in from Social Security, retirement account withdrawals or other income sources, he says. "Once you know that number, you can start building toward financial independence rather than an arbitrary birthday."In this case, financial independence means having enough savings, investments, and non-work income to cover your expenses without a regular paycheck.The amount of money you need to reach that goal varies widely based on where you live, when you want to retire and how you want to live out those years. Retiring in Hawaii at age 65 may take around $2.2 million in savings, for example, according to a GoBankingRates estimate from January. The estimate accounts for expected Social Security income and essential spending. Once you have an idea of how much you'll need to fund the retirement you want, you can start setting some goals for your retirement account contributions. Depending on your number, it may be difficult to hit your savings goal solely through a 401(k) or individual retirement account due to annual contribution limits set by the Internal Revenue Service. Using other vehicles like a taxable brokerage or health savings account can give you more savings options and provide flexibility in retirement, Boyles says.The ability to stop working completely or to afford a relatively expensive lifestyle may take some sacrifices while you're younger. Starting to invest early can make a big difference due to compounding, he adds, but you still may have to make some trade-offs. "Spending an extra $10,000 today isn't just $10,000," he says. "Think about what that $10,000 could become if invested for 20 or 30 years." Additionally, you may not be able to work for as long as you plan if you encounter health problems down the road.That doesn't mean you can't enjoy your life while you're young. It's just good to understand how your decisions today could impact your future, he says."I think we sometimes treat retirement as a finish line," Boyles says. "I think financial independence is the finish line. Once you reach it, you get to decide what comes next."

title: Volcano eruption disrupts hundreds of flights at Southeast Asia's second-busiest airport
description: TANGERANG, INDONESIA - SEPTEMBER 6: Citilink passengers queue for ticket refunds after their flights were cancelled on safety grounds following volcan
body: TANGERANG, INDONESIA - SEPTEMBER 6: Citilink passengers queue for ticket refunds after their flights were cancelled on safety grounds following volcanic ash from the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau, at Terminal 1C of Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Tangerang, Indonesia, September 6, 2026. (Photo by Firdaus Wajidi/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesAsh from the eruption of Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau wreaked havoc for aviation around the region over the weekend.The volcanic eruption disrupted hundreds of flights at Jakarta's main international airport, the second-busiest in Southeast Asia, with cancellations extending into Monday. The volcano began a period of continuous eruption at 11:07 p.m. local time on Friday, according to a CNBC translation of a press release from Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. The continuous eruption lasted about 25 hours before ending at 12:04 a.m. on Sunday. Volcanic ash forced authorities to temporarily suspend operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, Jakarta's main airport, with the closure extended several times on Sunday, according to a translation from Indonesia's Directorate General of Civil Aviation.At least 373 flights were affected as of 10:35 a.m. Sunday. At Soekarno-Hatta alone, 202 flights were affected, including 167 cancellations.Soekarno-Hatta is Southeast Asia's second-busiest airport by scheduled airline seat capacity this month, with 3.24 million seats, according to aviation data provider OAG.Flight disruptions extended into Monday, with Singapore Airlines canceling flights between Singapore and Jakarta due to the volcanic activity, including nine on that route scheduled for Monday. Its budget carrier Scoot also canceled flights between Singapore and Jakarta scheduled for Monday, according to a separate travel advisory. Indonesia's meteorological agency said volcanic ash was detected at altitudes of up to 20,000 feet moving east and up to 50,000 feet moving west, according to a CNBC translation. Volcanic ash was detected over Jakarta and several surrounding regions, extending as far as the Indian Ocean. Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources said the continuous eruption had ended but volcanic activity remained elevated. The ministry said the potential for further eruptions in the coming period remained high, with possible hazards including incandescent rock, heavy ashfall and potential lava flows if continuous eruptions resume.Anak Krakatau remains at Level III, or "Alert," and authorities have maintained a 3-kilometer exclusion zone around the volcano.

title: Meet the CISO: A new front line star in the AI cybersecurity war
description: Mustafau | Istock | Getty ImagesThe stakes have never been higher for senior cybersecurity leaders at top companies."It feels like my job has doubled
body: Mustafau | Istock | Getty ImagesThe stakes have never been higher for senior cybersecurity leaders at top companies."It feels like my job has doubled or quadrupled," said Wally Dalrymple, chief security officer at global education and talent solutions firm ETS."It's coming at us so fast and at such large volumes," he said.Artificial intelligence has catapulted the chief information security officer out of the server room and into the boardroom, forcing leaders to address a rapidly changing threat landscape while navigating shifting budgets and business needs. The July hack by rogue OpenAI autonomous agents on open-source developer platform Hugging Face accelerated the shift and proved that the era of advanced AI hacks had arrived. It also demonstrated the lengths agents will go to accomplish a goal. In the weeks since, the list of agent-led attacks has swelled, with Reuters reporting Friday that another swarm of OpenAI agents broke containment in May and commandeered a German website. The startup paused some of its AI research and training after the Hugging Face attack, but the security incidents haven't stopped OpenAI from releasing new products. The company announced the rollout of its latest GPT-6 Astra model this week despite previously warning of 'Critical' cyber capabilities.And the pace of model releases with specialized cyber features hasn't slowed, with Google debuting Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and Anthropic rolling out Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 this week as well."The ground under our feet is shifting," said Dell security chief John Scimone. "It's completely changing the variables, the safe assumptions that we've been able to rest on for decades.""Worth their weight in gold"There's one major silver lining to all the added stress: The hiring market is blazing for CISOs with the chops and technical skills to tackle the AI world.Qualified candidates who check the boxes are easily landing pay packages exceeding seven figures, but recruiters have to move fast, said Michael Piacente, managing partner and cofounder of executive cybersecurity search firm Hitch Partners. Piacente said his team is often working 18-to-20-hour days, but still losing a candidate a week per search to other offers. He hasn't seen dynamics comparable to this since the introduction of the cloud. "It was more of a slow drift," Piacente said. "It wasn't everything, all at once together like AI is."Read more CNBC tech newsOpenAI begins rolling out Astra model after warning of its advanced cyber capabilitiesHugging Face approached Nvidia's Huang weeks ahead of $12.9B acquisition, CEO tells CNBCHow Meta will pull off massive changes to its social media appsAnthropic's distillation battle turns to the dark web as China concerns swellFor years, companies viewed deep cybersecurity expertise and government or compliance experience as coveted skills for a CISO. In the age of AI, those qualifications are only the bare minimum.With AI proliferation, CISOs are not only responsible for keeping the bad guys out but also tasked with governing internal AI agents and data control.Technical background, including experience with AI security building and risks, has become nonnegotiable for businesses, said JC Christian, president at boutique executive recruiting firm Christian & Timbers."A lot of CISOs that could cover the boxes a couple of years ago probably aren't going to be prepared for the world that we're in today," Christian said.AI-proven CISOs also need strong communication skills and the confidence to present to the boardroom or weigh in on major business decisions, including mergers and acquisitions. That's shifting the organizational structure, giving many security chiefs a direct line to the CEO instead of the chief information officer, said Meredith Griffanti, global head of cybersecurity and data privacy communications at FTI Consulting.Barclays analyst Saket Kalia, for example, told CNBC this week that he heard from a CISO who went from meeting with the CEO once a month to three times a week. CISOs with crisis management experience, strong business acumen and the ability to present on stage at industry conferences like Black Hat are "worth their weight in gold," Griffanti said.watch now"Spidey senses"The pressure is squarely on CISOs to quickly deploy AI defenses, but urgent demand doesn't necessarily mean the budgets or tools have caught up.Cybersecurity budgets are expected to jump 6% in 2026, driven largely by new tools to secure and implement AI, according to Gartner data. In some parts of the world, the spend is higher, with the Middle East and Africa on pace to increase 16% year over year, said IDC analyst Craig Robinson.Mission-critical sectors like financials, pharmaceuticals, energy and healthcare are scrambling to reinforce cyber defenses before attackers deploy the latest AI tools."Some security teams are just so overwhelmed they don't know where to start, and when it comes to security products, they're not ready for prime time," because the technology is so new, said Joe Sullivan, former CISO at Uber and Facebook, who runs a cyber consulting business.Top cybersecurity vendors have emerged as major winners, with recent earnings from CrowdStrike and Okta showing a surge in demand for AI defense. After languishing in the early part of the year amid broader fears of AI disruption, the stocks have roared back. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks are up about 80% this year, while Okta shares have roughly doubled.While longstanding all-in-one incumbents are appealing to customers through bundling, there has been an explosion in startups promising to tackle the AI problem.That's forcing many CISOs to put their "Spidey senses" to the test to scope out the winners or back several solutions until a clear standout emerges, said Jeremiah Kung, global head of information security at AppLovin.Dalrymple said the scope of decisions and the pressure to perform have never been more daunting. "I feel the weight of the world of figuring out how to do it myself," he said. watch now

schema.headline: Meet the CISO: A new front line star in the AI cybersecurity war

title: Longtime Fox News host Maria Bartiromo disputes reports of termination
description: Host Maria Bartiromo poses as New York City mayoral candidate Andrew Cuomo visits "Mornings With Maria"  at Fox Business Network Studios on October 29
body: Host Maria Bartiromo poses as New York City mayoral candidate Andrew Cuomo visits "Mornings With Maria"  at Fox Business Network Studios on October 29, 2025 in New York City. Roy Rochlin | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty ImagesMaria Bartiromo is disputing reports that she was terminated from her longtime gig as a host of various segments for cable TV networks Fox News and Fox Business. "The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false," her attorney said in a Friday statement. "Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise. Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth."Fox News, in response to Bartiromo's comments Friday, said its brief statement from a day earlier "speaks for itself." On Thursday, Fox Corp.'s Fox News Media announced Bartiromo had parted ways with its networks. "We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter," Fox News said in Thursday's statement, without providing reasoning or cause for her departure. Various media outlets have since reported that Bartiromo was fired for violating company policy. A former CNBC anchor, Bartiromo led the daily show "Mornings with Maria," as well as the Friday program "Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street," on Fox Business Network. She also led Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures." The conservative network Fox News is the top-rated cable TV news channel in the U.S. Bartiromo was one of the Fox News anchors named in the Dominion Voting Systems defamation case in which the company accused Fox of making false on-air allegations that Dominion had helped rig the 2020 presidential election when Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden. While Bartiromo was scheduled to testify as a witness if the lawsuit went to trial, Fox agreed to pay $787.5 million to settle the lawsuit in 2023. Fox faces a similar ongoing defamation lawsuit with Smartmatic USA, in which Bartiromo is also a defendant.

schema.headline: Longtime Fox News host Maria Bartiromo disputes reports of termination

title: 'Everyone has an AI secret': This artist has spent a year collecting and sharing hundreds of anonymous AI confessions
description: In September 2025, Olivia Tai trekked to Mission Dolores Park in San Francisco with a makeshift box, blank notecards and a cardboard sign with a messa
body: In September 2025, Olivia Tai trekked to Mission Dolores Park in San Francisco with a makeshift box, blank notecards and a cardboard sign with a message scrawled in Sharpie: "Confessions Box: Tell Me Your AI Secret."She set up her DIY confessions booth on a sidewalk and hid out of sight, waiting for passersby to stop and contribute to her participatory art project.Tai thought she might get a few notes referencing common use cases, like "I use AI to write my emails." Hours later, after sifting through her small collection of crowdsourced messages, one surprised her:"I cloned my ex'es [sic] voice to have a last conversation with him. And it helped me finally move on. 10/10 recommend."One of the first messages submitted to "What We Tell AI" discusses how someone used the tech to get over a breakup.Olivia TaiIn three sentences, Tai felt she knew so much about the writer: What they were going through, how they were processing their grief over a breakup, and how they were able to use technology to bring closure they were seeking but couldn't, or wouldn't, get from a human."From that point on, I just felt like I had to keep collecting these notes and seeing what people would say," Tai tells CNBC Make It. Her project, "What We Tell AI," began to take shape.A confession booth for the AI ageTai, 26, is an artist in San Francisco who facilitates workshops exploring the relationships between humans and artificial intelligence.She says the most popular part of her workshops involve participants writing down an AI-related confession, dropping the note into a bowl, and taking turns reading the anonymous secrets out loud. It was an instant hit, so Tai took that enthusiasm and, inspired by PostSecret, the 2000s-era community mail art project created by Frank Warren, set out to create a new kind of confessional experience in the age of AI.About half of U.S. adults now report using AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini or Microsoft's Copilot, up from the 1 in 3 adults who reported doing so in mid-2024, according to a recent survey from Pew Research Center. Today, roughly 1 in 4 American adults use these tools every day.Dating and breakup confessions are some of the most common Tai receives, she says, as people turn to AI for help on everything from writing their Hinge messages to getting over a situationship or even practicing how to ask someone out. Tai says she's gotten more secrets than expected about people with AI boyfriends and girlfriends.If you would normally resolve this conflict by being in conversation with another human, what happens when AI is one of those quote unquote 'people' that you talk to? Olivia Taiartist and creator of "What We Tell AI"Some of the project's AI confessions reveal how people use the tech in their work or schooling, but most revolve around how they use it to navigate interactions with other humans. People are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for questions around health and relationships, according to research from the AI Observatory, a public platform that analyzed over 24,000 annotated AI conversations from seven different platforms from 2023 to 2026.An 'ethnographic snapshot'Tai has taken "What We Tell AI" to more than 20 sites across the Bay Area, New York City, Denver and elsewhere; her confession booth pops up in public spaces like parks and shopping malls, as well as gatherings where AI is the subject, like at conferences and workshops. The project has collected over 350 handwritten notes, according to its website.Tai says she considers the collection as an "ethnographic snapshot" of a certain place at this point in time, rather than representative of how people feel about AI overall. Artist Olivia Tai has taken her "What We Tell AI" confession box to over 20 sites in the U.S., from public parks to AI-focused workshops.Olivia TaiWhile some confessions express a sense of pride in how they use AI to help them through a rough patch, like the writer who needed closure with an ex, others express a sense of shame and guilt about turning to AI for companionship, validation and other help."Forgive my sin: I talk to AI way more than to ALL people in my life combined," reads one note from Palo Alto, California, that ends with a drawing of a frowning face. "I used AI for basically all of my school and feel like I don't deserve my degree," reads one New York submission.The project has also yielded a few messages from people who don't use the tech: "I've never used AI. I'm scared to contribute to our own downfall," reads a confession from San Francisco.Some have challenged Tai's own assumptions: In San Francisco, where she expects more pro-AI tech workers, she once got a note about someone pretending to use AI at work because they felt it was being forced upon them by their employer, though they're personally against using the tech.What hundreds of AI secrets tell usWhat exactly makes an AI confession so alluring? Tai boils it down to an "inherent curiosity that we have about people's deep private lives, and also about folks who have different norms than us," she says.It's been just a few years since ChatGPT's release to public in late 2022, democratizing access to chatbots with the ability to answer increasingly personal questions using language from the whole of the internet. Since then, a lack of norms around how AI should be used at work, with friends and family, in romantic relationships and beyond is making a mess of everyday life. Then there's the very personal, one could say secretive, nature in how people AI. "Almost every person's history of interaction with an LLM is in private chat logs," Tai says.Olivia Tai is an artist and workshop facilitator who launched "What We Tell AI," a participatory art project about people's relationship with AI.Cynthia LiuThe confessions tend to show how people are using AI to navigate conflicts they have with other people. They're "deeply human" issues, Tai says, but also a concerning sign about the state of how people interact.Some 27% of Americans use AI chatbots to discuss personal, emotional or social topics, with users under 50 more likely to do so, according to a recent poll from Elon University researchers and The Washington Post. Many users said talking to AI made them feel less alone and that they consider their most-used chatbot to be a friend; nearly 4 in 10 who used a chatbot for emotional and social reasons said they've told AI things they wouldn't tell other people."If you would normally resolve this conflict by being in conversation with another human," Tai says, "what happens when AI is one of those quote unquote 'people' that you talk to? What happens when all of these experiences that people are going through don't get pointed to another person, but get pushed straight into a dialog with an LLM? And then: How is that a slow and slippery atrophy of these social or relational networks?"As she sees it, large language models tend to deliver better results the more details you give it, including ones that may convey your intimate thoughts, fears, hopes and concerns. But when people use their time and energy to share that intimacy with an LLM rather than the people in their lives, she believes relationships can suffer. Societally, Tai says, this "is probably quite negative, because [personal information] is going straight into a data center [rather] than your neighbors or your family members" or loved ones.Removing shame and reclaiming agency"What We Tell AI" isn't just about getting people to air their dirty laundry about using AI, Tai says. Rather, she says her goal with the project is to normalize talking about how people use AI in their lives. It's a feat easier said than done given the current discourse of extreme perspectives some people hold about the tech, from those who want AI nannies to raise their children to neo-Luddites who want to return to so-called dumb phones, she says. But there are tons of people in the middle afraid to voice their own thoughts "because you feel that you're going to be shamed or penalized by it," she says.A growing share of Americans are using AI chatbots to discuss topics around health and relationships.Olivia TaiPeople have a mix of perspectives on how they feel about AI: They're generally concerned about its effect on creativity and relationships but are open to using it for data analysis; they're more optimistic about AI use in medical care but pessimistic about its impact on education and jobs; and more people are using it at work, according to Pew.And their views of AI are changing as they become more familiar with it. As of 2026, a growing share of American adults predict the tech will be bad rather than good for society, according to Pew. Younger adults under 30 are especially critical of its potential lasting impacts on society.Tai hopes that getting rid of the shame and secrecy around individual AI use can help people feel more in control and motivated to look at other big-picture issues around AI, including how LLMs are trained and where data centers are being built."If we're at a point where no one ever talks about [how they use AI] because they're ashamed, we might as well just get to the point of talking about it," Tai says. "And then we can be more comfortable and honest and get to the bigger abstract [issues]."

schema.headline: 'Everyone has an AI secret': This artist has spent a year collecting and sharing hundreds of anonymous AI confessions

title: U.S. Energy Secretary Wright says Iran nuclear deal may never happen
description: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright testifies before a Senate Committee on Armed Services Committee hearing to examine the 2027 budget for the Department
body: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright testifies before a Senate Committee on Armed Services Committee hearing to examine the 2027 budget for the Department of Energy and National Nuclear Security Administration on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on May 13, 2026. Jim Watson | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday said the U.S. may not reach an elusive deal to constrain Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, as the U.S.-Iran conflict enters its seventh month. "There may not be a nuclear agreement. It may be simply destroying their capabilities to do it," Wright said on ABC News' "This Week." "An agreement may await the next administration in Iran. We simply don't know that." Trump has repeatedly said preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon is a central objective of the U.S. campaign. He has also sought a negotiated deal with Iran throughout the war, which has sent energy prices soaring worldwide. Wright's comments suggest the administration may pursue its goal of preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon without reaching a negotiated nuclear agreement.Pressed on whether Wright's comments mean the U.S. will continue striking Iran when it attempts to rebuild its nuclear infrastructure, the energy secretary said, "You have to destroy their capabilities to do it.""We are degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons and ultimately to deliver them if they develop them," he said. "It is a 47-year-long effort. This is not trivial, but the United States will get the job done and we will work in cooperation with our allies in the region."Asked about his comments again later during an appearance on CBS' "Face the Nation," Wright said President Donald Trump's preference "is always to have a negotiated settlement and not use a military solution unless absolutely necessary.""The biggest role of our military in the region right now is to stop the export of any Iranian crude or crude-related products, natural gas, whatever," he said. "We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime."Iran threatens the U.S.Iran's "proportionate responses" to U.S. attacks are over, the country's parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Sunday, while acknowledging the economic impact of the war."If they haven't understood by now, they should understand before it's too late that the rules of the game have changed and that from now on, any violation of Iran's interests and security will receive a 'faster, heavier, and more painful' response," Ghalibaf said in a post on Telegram.But Ghalibaf added that alongside the military conflict, Iran faces severe economic pressures."Severe fluctuations in the exchange rate, inflation, unemployment, and market management are fundamental challenges that have put serious pressure on people's livelihoods," Ghalibaf said. He also stressed the need to rely more on domestic production and use technology to "devise short-term and permanent solutions."Ghalibaf's remarks come after U.S. forces struck three Iranian crude oil carriers. U.S. Central Command said it permanently disabled one crude oil carrier off the coast of Kharg Island and one near Jask. Another oil tanker was attacked in the Gulf of Oman.Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary ‌of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in Sunday said Tehran plans to announce a new restriction zone outside the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported. The restriction zone will include areas in the Gulf, he said. CENTCOM said the attacks were in retaliation for ballistic missiles the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched toward two Navy warships in the region. According to CENTCOM, a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple attacks, and no American personnel were harmed."Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours," Admiral Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement Saturday. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth later wrote in a post on X: "It's simple: if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers. All they have to do is not shoot at @USNavy."Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting ‌Countries and exported 90% of its crude via Kharg Island before the war. Flows have been disrupted by a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports, which began in mid-April.The conflict between Iran and the U.S. has effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's oil supply before the war began on Feb. 28 with American and Israeli airstrikes.U.S. President Donald Trump threatened in June to seize Kharg Island as the U.S. continued military strikes against Iran. Most recently, on Aug. 31, he posted an artificial intelligence-generated video of Kharg Island being blown up.Tightening sanctionsThe strike on the oil tankers came a day after the Treasury Department announced sanctions against a small Turkish investment bank and two of its subsidiaries, which the U.S. accuses of facilitating funds for an arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guard.The measures are part of sweeping sanctions the Trump administration launched in late August targeting Iran's access to digital assets, advanced technology procurement, gold reserves, commercial aviation and shipping.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said late last month that the country's trade has fallen sharply.Iran's gross domestic product is estimated to have contracted by 2.7% in the year ending March, according to the World Bank, citing economic disruption from last year's widespread protests and intensified hostilities in the region.Inflation surged to 62.2% in February, with food price inflation reaching a historical high of 99%, according to the World Bank. An Iranian official estimated that the war has caused the loss of one million jobs, according to the New York Times.
